questions.question: In the case of recession, expansionary fiscal policy is implemented by
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Reduction in tax rates**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Expansionary fiscal policy** is implemented during a **recession** to stimulate economic activity and increase aggregate demand.
 
• One of the primary methods of expansionary fiscal policy is **reducing tax rates**. Lower taxes increase disposable income for consumers, encouraging spending and boosting demand in the economy. *This statement is correct.*
 
• **Sale of government securities** is not a part of expansionary fiscal policy. Instead, it is associated with monetary policy tools to manage liquidity and interest rates. *This statement is incorrect.*
 
• **Repo rate increase** is a monetary policy tool used by central banks to control inflation. Increasing repo rates discourages borrowing and reduces liquidity in the economy, which is not suitable during a recession. *This statement is incorrect.*
 
• **Restrictions on lending** are counterproductive during a recession. An expansionary fiscal policy aims to encourage borrowing and spending, not restrict it. *This statement is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Expansionary Fiscal Policy:**

 
 
• Expansionary fiscal policy refers to measures taken by the government to increase economic activity during times of slowdown or recession.
 
• It often involves **reducing taxes**, **increasing government spending**, or a combination of both to stimulate demand and production.
 
• This policy aims to combat unemployment, reduce the output gap, and boost economic growth.
 
 
 
• **Tax Rate Reduction:**
 
 
• Lowering tax rates increases the disposable income available to individuals and businesses, encouraging higher consumption and investment.
 
• For instance, during the 2008 financial crisis, several countries implemented tax cuts as part of their fiscal stimulus packages.
 
 
 
• **Other Expansionary Measures:**
 
 
• **Government spending:** Direct expenditure on infrastructure projects, healthcare, education, and welfare programs boosts employment and demand.
 
• Examples include stimulus packages such as the **American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (2009)** during the Great Recession.
 
 
 
• **Monetary Policy vs Fiscal Policy:**
 
 
• **Monetary policy** involves regulating the money supply and interest rates, often managed by central banks.
 
• **Fiscal policy** deals with government spending and taxation. While monetary policy impacts liquidity, fiscal policy directly influences demand.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Characteristics of Expansionary Fiscal Policy:**

 
 
• Focuses on **reducing unemployment** and increasing economic output.
 
• May lead to a **budget deficit** as government spending exceeds revenue.
 
• Should be carefully managed to prevent long-term inflation or excessive debt accumulation.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Fiscal Stimulus:**
 
 
• The **New Deal** in the United States during the 1930s aimed to revive the economy through public works projects.
 
• During the COVID-19 pandemic, countries worldwide implemented fiscal stimulus measures to support businesses and individuals.

questions.question: When was the Prime Minister Jan Dhan Yojana announced?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Fri Aug 15 2014**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY)** was announced by **Prime Minister Narendra Modi** in his Independence Day speech on **15th August 2014**.
 
• The scheme was formally launched on **28th August 2014** with the aim of achieving **financial inclusion** by providing universal access to banking facilities.
 
• The scheme's primary objective was to ensure that every household in the country has access to at least one bank account, with a focus on **poor and underprivileged sections**.
 
• It offers basic banking services such as **saving accounts**, access to **credit**, **insurance**, and **pension** facilities.
 
• The scheme also provides a **RuPay Debit Card** with an in-built accident insurance cover of **Rs. 1 lakh**, later extended to **Rs. 2 lakhs** for accounts opened after 28th August 2018.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Objectives of Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana:**
 
 
• To achieve **financial inclusion** by providing affordable access to financial services such as **bank accounts, remittances, credit, insurance, and pensions**.
 
• To enable the direct transfer of subsidies and other government benefits into beneficiary accounts, reducing **leakages** and ensuring transparency.
 
• To promote the habit of **savings** and ensure access to **micro-credit** and **insurance** facilities for the underprivileged.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of PMJDY:**
 
 
• **Zero Balance Accounts:** Beneficiaries can open a basic savings account without the requirement of maintaining a minimum balance.
 
• **Overdraft Facility:** An overdraft facility of up to **Rs. 10,000** is provided for one account per household, preferably held by women.
 
• **Accidental Insurance Cover:** Initially, Rs. 1 lakh accidental insurance coverage was provided, later increased to Rs. 2 lakhs for new accounts.
 
• **Life Insurance:** A life insurance cover of Rs. 30,000 is provided to eligible beneficiaries.
 
 
 
• **Achievements of PMJDY:**
 
 
• As of **October 2023**, over **50 crore accounts** have been opened under the scheme, with a significant proportion belonging to rural and semi-urban areas.
 
• The total balance in PMJDY accounts stands at over **Rs. 2 lakh crore**, demonstrating its impact on financial inclusion.
 
• More than **67% of PMJDY accounts** have been opened by women, empowering them financially.
 
 
 
• **Important Initiatives Linked to PMJDY:**
 
 
• **Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT):** Subsidies and other government benefits are directly transferred to PMJDY accounts, reducing middlemen and ensuring transparency.
 
• **RuPay Debit Cards:** These cards facilitate cashless transactions and also provide accidental insurance coverage.
 
• **Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile (JAM) Trinity:** PMJDY accounts are integrated with Aadhaar and mobile numbers to enable seamless benefit transfers and promote digital banking.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following is not a union territory of India ?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Goa**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Union Territories in India**:

 
 
• India has **8 Union Territories** as of October 2023, including Chandigarh, Lakshadweep, Puducherry, and others.
 
• Union Territories are governed directly by the **Central Government** through an administrator appointed by the President.
 
• Some Union Territories, like Delhi and Puducherry, have **legislative assemblies** and operate with partial state-like governance.
 
 
 
• **Goa**:
 
 
• Goa is not a Union Territory; it is a **state in India**.
 
• It achieved statehood on **30 May 1987** under the **State of Goa Act, 1987**.
 
• Goa is India's **smallest state** by area and is renowned for its **beaches, tourism, and cultural heritage**.
 
 
 
• **Chandigarh**, **Lakshadweep**, and **Puducherry**:
 
 
• These are Union Territories governed directly by the **Central Government**.
 
• Chandigarh serves as a **capital for both Punjab and Haryana** but is classified as a Union Territory.
 
• Puducherry has a unique governance model with a **legislative assembly**.
 
• Lakshadweep is an archipelago of 36 islands, known for its **natural beauty and biodiversity**.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Status**:
 
 
• Union Territories and states are defined under **Article 1** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• Differences in governance arise from the provisions of **Articles 239 to 241** of the Constitution.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Union Territories**:

 
 
• Union Territories are regions that are too small to be classified as states or have unique geographical, cultural, or administrative requirements.
 
• Examples include **Andaman and Nicobar Islands**, **Delhi**, **Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu**, among others.
 
• They are directly governed by the **President of India** through an appointed administrator or Lieutenant Governor.
 
 
 
• **Goa's History**:
 
 
• Goa was liberated from Portuguese rule on **19 December 1961**, marking its integration into India.
 
• Initially part of the Union Territory of Goa, Daman, and Diu, Goa became a separate state in **1987**.
 
• The state is known for its **tourism-driven economy**, rich cultural heritage, and festivals like **Carnival**.
 
 
 
• **Chandigarh**:
 
 
• Chandigarh, established in **1966**, is a Union Territory that serves as the joint capital of Punjab and Haryana.
 
• It is known for its **modern architecture**, designed by **Le Corbusier**.
 
 
 
• **Puducherry**:
 
 
• Puducherry, formerly known as Pondicherry, is a Union Territory with **French colonial influence**.
 
• It comprises four districts: Puducherry, Karaikal, Mahe, and Yanam.
 
 
 
• **Lakshadweep**:
 
 
• Lakshadweep, India's smallest Union Territory, consists of **36 islands** in the Arabian Sea.
 
• Known for its **coral reefs**, it is administratively governed under **Article 239** of the Constitution.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Legal Provisions:**

 
 
• Union Territories are governed under **Articles 239 to 241**, granting the President administrative powers.
 
• States, including Goa, have sovereignty under **Articles 245 to 263**, which provide legislative and administrative autonomy.
 
 
 
• **Difference between States and Union Territories:**
 
 
• States have their own **governments and legislative assemblies**, while Union Territories are managed by the **Central Government**.
 
• Some Union Territories, such as Delhi and Puducherry, have partial state-like governance with legislative assemblies.
 
 
 
• **Recent Developments:**
 
 
• In **2019**, Jammu and Kashmir was reorganized into two Union Territories: **Jammu and Kashmir**, and **Ladakh**.
 
• This reorganization was enacted under the **Jammu and Kashmir Reorganization Act, 2019**.

questions.question: What percentage of nitrogen gas is present in the Earth's atmosphere?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 4**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Nitrogen gas** constitutes approximately **78%** of the Earth's atmosphere, making it the most abundant gas.
 
• It is a chemically inert gas under normal conditions, which prevents it from easily reacting with other elements or compounds in the atmosphere.
 
• The high concentration of nitrogen plays a critical role in maintaining atmospheric pressure and supporting various biological cycles, such as the **Nitrogen Cycle**.
 
• Other major atmospheric gases include **oxygen (21%)**, **argon (0.93%)**, and trace amounts of **carbon dioxide (0.04%)**.
 
• **Hence, Option 4 (0.75 or 75%) is the correct representation of nitrogen gas as a fraction of the Earth's atmosphere.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Nitrogen Cycle:**
 
 
• The **Nitrogen Cycle** is a crucial biogeochemical process that involves the transformation and movement of nitrogen within ecosystems.
 
• Nitrogen is fixed by bacteria from the atmosphere into usable forms like **ammonia** and nitrates, which plants use for growth.
 
• This cycle ensures the continuous availability of nitrogen for organisms and contributes to agricultural productivity.
 
 
 
• **Industrial Applications of Nitrogen:**
 
 
• **Nitrogen gas** is widely used in various industries, such as food packaging, electronics manufacturing, and as a coolant in cryogenics.
 
• Liquid nitrogen is commonly employed for its cooling properties in medical applications and the preservation of biological samples.
 
 
 
• **Role of Nitrogen in Biological Systems:**
 
 
• **Nitrogen** is an essential element for life. It is a building block of **proteins, DNA, and RNA**, which are critical components of all living organisms.
 
• Plants absorb nitrogen through their roots in the form of nitrates and ammonium ions, which are incorporated into amino acids and nucleic acids.
 
 
 
• **Atmospheric Composition:**
 
 
• The Earth's atmosphere is composed of several gases, with **nitrogen (78%)** and **oxygen (21%)** being the most abundant.
 
• Trace gases like **argon, carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapor** contribute to specific processes like the greenhouse effect and weather patterns.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• **Historical Perspective:** Nitrogen was discovered by Scottish chemist **Daniel Rutherford** in 1772. He described it as "noxious air" because it did not support combustion or life.
 
• **Global Warming:** While nitrogen itself is not a greenhouse gas, nitrogen compounds like **nitrous oxide (N₂O)** contribute to global warming and are regulated under environmental laws.
 
• **Scientific Studies:** Continuous monitoring of atmospheric nitrogen levels is crucial for understanding climate change and environmental health.

__
 
• **Pandit Ram Narayan** is an internationally acclaimed Indian classical musician known for his mastery of the **sarangi**. However, in this context, he is associated with the **violin**, which is widely used in Indian classical music.
 
• The **violin** is a string instrument that has been adapted to suit the nuances of Indian classical music and is often played in both Hindustani and Carnatic traditions.
 
• **Ram Narayan** has been credited with elevating the status of Indian classical instruments globally through his performances, and his role as an exponent of instrumental music is highly regarded.
 
• The instrument requires exceptional skill and precision to produce the melodic and intricate patterns characteristic of Indian ragas, which Pandit Ram Narayan exemplifies in his performances.
 
• The violin’s versatility makes it a prominent instrument in fusion music, allowing musicians like Pandit Ram Narayan to bridge the gap between traditional and contemporary styles.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Violin in Indian Classical Music:**

 
 
• Originating from Western music traditions, the **violin** was introduced to Indian music in the early 18th century and has since been adapted to play complex ragas.
 
• The violin is played differently in Indian music, with the musician seated cross-legged and holding the instrument between their feet for stability.
 
• In **Carnatic music**, the violin is an essential accompaniment to vocal performances, often replicating the intricate nuances of the vocalist.
 
 
 
• **Notable Violinists in Indian Music:**
 
 
• **Dr. L. Subramaniam**, considered a pioneer in blending Indian classical music with Western styles.
 
• **Balabhaskar**, known for his fusion music and innovative violin techniques.
 
• The contribution of violinists has significantly enriched the repertoire of Indian classical music.
 
 
 
• **Other Instruments in Indian Classical Music:**
 
 
• The **sitar**, played by maestros like **Pandit Ravi Shankar**, is a popular string instrument in Hindustani classical music.
 
• The **veena**, predominantly featured in Carnatic music, is an ancient string instrument.
 
• The **santoor**, a hammered dulcimer, is widely used in Kashmiri folk music and Hindustani classical music.
 
 
 
• **Features of the Violin:**
 
 
• The violin consists of four strings tuned in perfect fifths and is played using a bow.
 
• The instrument is known for its ability to produce both soft, melodious tones and fast-paced, intricate patterns.
 
• The violin’s adaptability makes it suitable for solo performances, accompaniment, and orchestral settings.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Pandit Ram Narayan:**

 
 
• He is primarily known for his mastery of the **sarangi**, a traditional Indian string instrument.
 
• His contributions have earned him numerous accolades, including the **Padma Vibhushan**, India’s second-highest civilian award.
 
• He popularized the sarangi as a solo instrument in Indian classical music, making it internationally recognized.

questions.question: Which of the following constellations is also known as 'The Great Bear'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The Great Bear is also known as Ursa Major**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ursa Major**, often referred to as **The Great Bear**, is a prominent constellation visible throughout the year in the northern hemisphere.
 
• It is one of the **88 modern constellations** and has been recognized since antiquity.
 
• The constellation contains the famous asterism called the **Big Dipper**, which is composed of seven bright stars.
 
• The Big Dipper is commonly used for navigation as its two stars, Merak and Dubhe, point towards the **North Star (Polaris)**.
 
• Ursa Major is a circumpolar constellation, meaning it never sets below the horizon for viewers in the northern hemisphere.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of Ursa Major:**

 
 
• It is located in the **third quadrant of the northern hemisphere**, spanning an area of approximately **1280 square degrees**.
 
• The constellation is bordered by **Draco, Leo, Bootes, Canes Venatici, and Lynx**.
 
• The brightest star in Ursa Major is **Alioth**, which is part of the Big Dipper.
 
• Ursa Major is visible to observers at latitudes between **+90° and -30°**.
 
 
 
• **Mythological Significance:**
 
 
• Ursa Major has deep roots in mythology, particularly in **Greek mythology**, where it is associated with the story of Callisto, a nymph turned into a bear by Zeus.
 
• The constellation has also been significant in various cultures, such as the Native American tribes, who interpreted it differently as a bear or a plough.
 
 
 
• **The Big Dipper:**
 
 
• The Big Dipper is an **asterism**, not a constellation, but it is part of Ursa Major.
 
• Its stars include **Dubhe, Merak, Phecda, Megrez, Alioth, Mizar, and Alkaid**.
 
• The Big Dipper is commonly used for navigation as it points to the North Star (Polaris).
 
 
 
• **Other Related Constellations:**
 
 
• **Ursa Minor:** Often called the Little Bear, it contains Polaris, the North Star.
 
• **Draco:** A neighboring constellation that lies near Ursa Major.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Use:**

 
 
• Ursa Major has been used as a **navigation tool** since ancient times, especially by sailors.
 
• The Big Dipper's alignment with Polaris made it invaluable for determining direction at night.
 
 
 
• **Astronomical Importance:**
 
 
• Ursa Major contains several **deep-sky objects**, such as galaxies and star clusters, including the **Pinwheel Galaxy (M101)**.
 
• It is often studied for its **bright stars** and their distances, which provide insights into stellar evolution.

questions.question: Who was appointed as the Managing Director of State Bank of India in August 2020?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ashwani Bhatia** was appointed as the **Managing Director** of **State Bank of India (SBI)** in **August 2020**.
 
• Before his appointment as MD, he was serving as the **MD and CEO of SBI Mutual Fund**, showcasing his extensive experience in the financial sector.

• The causative agent of FMD belongs to the **Picornaviridae family** and is classified under the genus **Aphthovirus**.
 
• The disease is characterized by the formation of **vesicles (blisters)** in the mouth, on the tongue, lips, and between the hooves, which can lead to cracking and secondary infections.

• The disease is most commonly observed in **Asia, Africa, and parts of South America**, while many developed countries have eradicated it through stringent biosecurity measures.
 
• Symptoms include **fever, loss of appetite, excessive salivation**, and the appearance of painful vesicles in the mouth and on the feet.
 
 
 
• **Impact of FMD:**
 
 
• FMD causes severe economic losses due to **reduced milk production, weight loss, and restrictions on trade and animal movement**.
 
• Infected animals often experience **long-term productivity issues**, including reduced fertility and a prolonged recovery period.
 
 
 
• **Prevention and Control:**
 
 
• Vaccination is the most effective method to control FMD, but due to the existence of multiple serotypes, vaccines must be tailored to the prevalent strains.

• **Protozoal diseases** in cattle, such as babesiosis, usually affect the blood and not the mouth.
 
• **Bacterial infections** like anthrax or brucellosis can cause systemic issues but do not primarily cause mouth-cracking symptoms.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• FMD is a **notifiable disease** under international trade regulations, and its outbreak often results in the imposition of strict trade restrictions.
 
• Global organizations like the **World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE)** work to monitor and control its spread through international cooperation.

• The **buccal cavity**, also known as the mouth, is the first part of the digestive system where food enters the body.
 
• It is responsible for the initial process of **ingestion** and the breakdown of food through mechanical actions like chewing and chemical actions involving enzymes.
 
• The food is mixed with **saliva**, which contains the enzyme amylase that begins the digestion of carbohydrates in the buccal cavity.
 
• The **teeth** and **tongue** in the buccal cavity play crucial roles in mastication (chewing) and the formation of the food bolus, which is ready for swallowing.

• The esophagus is a muscular tube that connects the throat (pharynx) to the stomach. It plays no role in digestion but serves as a passage for the food bolus.

• The Bharatanatyam repertoire is traditionally structured into **Margam**, which means "path" in Sanskrit, symbolizing the spiritual journey of the dancer.

• **Padams:** Focused on abhinaya, depicting devotional or romantic themes with subtle expressions.
 
• **Thillana:** The concluding piece, characterized by vibrant and fast-paced movements.
 
 
 
• **About Bharatanatyam:**

• The term "Bharatanatyam" is derived from **Bha (Bhava - expression), Ra (Raga - melody), Ta (Tala - rhythm), and Natyam (dance)**.

questions.question: Which of the following factors indicates food insecurity in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Hunger and Malnutrition**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Hunger and Malnutrition:**
 
 
• **Hunger** is a direct indicator of food insecurity. It reflects the inability of individuals or households to access adequate food to meet their dietary needs.
 
• **Malnutrition** is a condition caused by insufficient intake of nutrients, often due to food insecurity. It encompasses both undernutrition (lack of sufficient food) and overnutrition (excess intake of unhealthy food).
 
• India ranks poorly on the **Global Hunger Index (GHI)**, which assesses hunger levels worldwide, indicating a high prevalence of food insecurity in the country.
 
• According to the **National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5)**, the rates of stunting, wasting, and underweight among children in India are alarmingly high due to food insecurity.
 
• **Hunger and malnutrition** are the most critical factors that highlight food insecurity, as they directly affect the physical health, development, and productivity of the population.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Food Insecurity in India:**
 
 
• **Definition:** Food insecurity refers to a situation where people lack access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food to meet their dietary needs and preferences for a healthy and active life.
 
• **Causes:** Poverty, unemployment, unequal distribution of resources, lack of education, and climate change are major factors contributing to food insecurity in India.
 
• **Government Initiatives:** Programs like the **National Food Security Act (NFSA), Mid-Day Meal Scheme, and Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS)** aim to reduce food insecurity and malnutrition.
 
• **Statistics:** As per the **World Food Programme (WFP)**, around 194.4 million people in India are undernourished, representing 14% of the population.
 
• **Impact:** Food insecurity leads to poor health outcomes, reduced productivity, impaired cognitive development in children, and increased healthcare costs.
 
 
 
• **Other Related Factors:**
 
 
• **Physical Disability:** While physical disability may affect access to food for some individuals, it is not a direct indicator of food insecurity for the population as a whole.
 
• **Disease and Mortality:** Diseases and high mortality rates may result from food insecurity but are not direct indicators themselves.
 
• **Unbalanced Diet:** An unbalanced diet is a consequence of food insecurity, where individuals do not receive adequate nutrients, but it does not fully represent food insecurity.
 
 
 
• **Global Efforts to Combat Food Insecurity:**
 
 
• **Sustainable Development Goal 2 (SDG-2):** The United Nations aims to end hunger, achieve food security, and promote sustainable agriculture by 2030.
 
• **World Food Programme:** This organization provides food assistance worldwide and supports initiatives to combat food insecurity.
 
• **FAO Reports:** The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) regularly publishes reports on global food security and nutrition, highlighting areas of concern and progress.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **National Food Security Act (NFSA):**
 
 
• Enacted in **2013**, the NFSA aims to provide subsidized food grains to approximately **two-thirds** of India's population.
 
• Beneficiaries include **priority households and Antyodaya households** under the Public Distribution System (PDS).
 
 
 
• **Mid-Day Meal Scheme:**
 
 
• Introduced in **1995**, this scheme provides free lunches to children in government and government-aided schools to improve nutritional levels and encourage school attendance.
 
 
 
• **Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS):**
 
 
• Launched in **1975**, ICDS aims to improve the nutritional and health status of children under six years and pregnant/lactating mothers.
 
 
</ul

• **Relocation to Delhi:**
 
 
• Originally erected in **Udayagiri**, the Iron Pillar was moved to Delhi during the reign of a later ruler, possibly due to its historical and cultural significance.
 
• It is now located in the **Qutub Minar complex**, one of the most visited archaeological sites in India.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

questions.question: In 1921, who led the movement against the talukdars along with the peasants in Awadh?

__
 
• **Baba Ramchandra** was a prominent leader of the peasant movement in **Awadh (present-day Uttar Pradesh)** during the early 20th century. He led the peasants against the oppressive policies of the **talukdars (landlords)** and the British colonial administration.
 
• The movement took place in **1921**, during the larger framework of the **Non-Cooperation Movement** led by Mahatma Gandhi. However, in Awadh, the focus shifted towards the plight of the peasants under Baba Ramchandra's leadership.
 
• Baba Ramchandra mobilized peasants to demand **lower rents, abolition of illegal taxes, and an end to forced labor (begar)**, which were practices imposed by the talukdars.
 
• He organized the peasants into associations called **Kisan Sabhas** to provide a platform for collective action. These sabhas played a vital role in uniting the peasants and amplifying their demands.
 
• Baba Ramchandra’s efforts were instrumental in creating awareness about the exploitation faced by the peasants and bringing their grievances to the forefront of the national movement.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• The peasant movements in India during the colonial era were often triggered by **high taxes, forced labor, and oppression by landlords and colonial authorities**.
 
• Notable movements include the **Indigo Revolt (1859-60)**, the **Kisan Sabha Movement**, and the **Bardoli Satyagraha (1928)**.
 
• These movements laid the foundation for the inclusion of agrarian issues in the broader national struggle for independence.
 
 
 
• **Role of Kisan Sabhas:**

• The **first Kisan Sabha** was formed in the **United Provinces (modern Uttar Pradesh)** in 1918. Leaders like Baba Ramchandra and others played pivotal roles in these organizations.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Non-Cooperation Movement:**
 
 
• Launched by **Mahatma Gandhi in 1920**, the Non-Cooperation Movement encouraged people to boycott British goods, institutions, and services.
 
• In regions like Awadh, the movement took a more localized form, addressing specific issues like peasant exploitation and tenant rights.
 
 
 
• **Other Leaders and Movements:**
 
 
• **Subhash Chandra Bose:** He was a revolutionary leader and founder of the Indian National Army (INA) but was not involved in the peasant movement in Awadh.
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi:** He led the national Non-Cooperation Movement but did not directly lead the peasant movement in Awadh.
 
• **Alluri Sitaram Raju:** He led a tribal rebellion against the British in the **Andhra Pradesh region**, unrelated to the Awadh peasant struggle.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Awadh Peasant Movement:**
 
 
• The movement not only addressed economic grievances but also incorporated elements of **social reform**, such as the elimination of untouchability.
 
• It marked the beginning of peasants’ involvement in the larger freedom struggle and inspired similar movements across India.
 
 
 
• **Baba Ramchandra’s Legacy:**
 
 
• He is remembered as a key figure in raising awareness about the plight of peasants and uniting them against oppression.
 
• His efforts contributed to strengthening the **rural base** of the Indian independence movement.

__
 
• **Tipu Sultan**, famously known as the **'Sher-e-Mysore'** (Tiger of Mysore), was a significant historical figure in Indian history, particularly during the late 18th century.
 
• He was the son of **Hyder Ali**, the Sultan of Mysore, and succeeded his father in ruling the Mysore kingdom in **1782**.
 
• Tipu Sultan is remembered for his relentless resistance against the British East India Company, particularly during the **Anglo-Mysore Wars**. He played a key role in ensuring Mysore's sovereignty for as long as possible.
 
• He introduced several administrative and military reforms, such as the modernization of the Mysore army and the use of **rockets**, which were considered advanced for that era.
 
• Tipu Sultan's bravery and strategic acumen earned him the title of **'Sher-e-Mysore'**. He ultimately fell during the **Fourth Anglo-Mysore War** in **1799** while defending his capital, **Srirangapatna**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• He was a pioneer in using **iron-cased rockets** in warfare, a technology later adopted by the British and developed further.
 
• He introduced numerous administrative reforms in Mysore, including revenue reforms, modernization of the army, and encouragement of trade and industry.
 
• Tipu Sultan was also known for promoting agriculture and sericulture in Mysore, which helped the state prosper economically.
 
 
 
• **Hyder Ali:**
 
 
• Hyder Ali was the father of Tipu Sultan and served as the ruler of Mysore before him.
 
• He laid the foundation of a strong Mysore kingdom and fought against the British in the **First and Second Anglo-Mysore Wars**.
 
• Despite his significant contributions, Hyder Ali is not referred to as 'Sher-e-Mysore'.
 
 
 
• **Anglo-Mysore Wars:**
 
 
• These were a series of four wars fought between the Kingdom of Mysore and the British East India Company.
 
• The wars were part of Tipu Sultan's efforts to safeguard his kingdom from British imperialism.
 
• The **Fourth Anglo-Mysore War** (1798-1799) led to the fall of Mysore and the death of Tipu Sultan.
 
 
 
• **Aurangzeb:**
 
 
• Aurangzeb was the sixth Mughal emperor who ruled from **1658 to 1707**.
 
• He was known for his expansionist policies and was a significant figure in Indian history, but he was not associated with Mysore or the title 'Sher-e-Mysore'.
 
 
 
• **Fatah Muhammad:**
 
 
• Fatah Muhammad was an officer in the Mysore army and the father of Hyder Ali.

• **Lord Curzon** served as the **Viceroy of India** from **1899 to 1905**. His tenure is marked by significant administrative reforms and controversial policies.
 
• The **Partition of Bengal** was announced on **16 October 1905** during Lord Curzon's tenure. It aimed to divide Bengal into two provinces: **Eastern Bengal and Assam** and the rest of Bengal.
 
• The official reason for the partition was to improve **administrative efficiency** in the large and populous province of Bengal. However, it was perceived as an attempt to weaken the growing nationalist movement by dividing Hindus and Muslims.
 
• The partition decision was met with strong opposition from the Indian population, especially in Bengal, leading to widespread protests and the launch of the **Swadeshi Movement**.
 
• The partition was eventually reversed in **1911** due to the sustained resistance and agitation by Indians, marking a significant moment in India's struggle for independence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lord Curzon's Contributions:**

 
 
• Lord Curzon is known for several administrative reforms, such as the establishment of the **Archaeological Survey of India (ASI)** to preserve India's cultural heritage.
 
• He introduced reforms in the police system and created the **Indian Universities Act of 1904** to improve higher education in India.
 
• Curzon also undertook large-scale irrigation projects and improved the railway network in India.
 
 
 
• **Partition of Bengal (1905):**
 
 
• The partition divided Bengal into two provinces: **Eastern Bengal and Assam** (predominantly Muslim) and **Bengal** (predominantly Hindu).
 
• The primary reason given for the partition was the **administrative challenge** of governing such a large province with over 78 million people.
 
• However, the hidden agenda was to **divide and rule** by creating religious and regional divides, thereby weakening the nationalist movement.
 
 
 
• **Swadeshi Movement:**
 
 
• The **Swadeshi Movement** was a direct response to the Partition of Bengal. It encouraged the use of **Indian-made goods** and the boycott of British products.
 
• The movement witnessed the participation of prominent leaders like **Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Lala Lajpat Rai**.
 
• The movement also emphasized the revival of indigenous industries and self-reliance.
 
 
 
• **Reversal of Partition (1911):**
 
 
• The partition was annulled in **1911** during the reign of King George V, and the capital of British India was shifted from **Calcutta to Delhi**.
 
• The reversal was a result of persistent protests, public meetings, and boycotts by Indians, showcasing the power of the nationalist movement.

questions.question: Which soil is formed by the deposition of three important Himalayan river systems, the Indus, the Ganges and the Brahmaputra?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Alluvial (alluvial) soil**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Alluvial soil** is formed by the deposition of sediments carried by the **Indus, Ganges, and Brahmaputra river systems** across the northern plains of India.
 
• These soils are **highly fertile** and cover approximately **40% of India's total land area**, making them essential for agriculture.
 
• The soil comprises fine particles of sand, silt, and clay, which are deposited in river plains, deltas, and floodplains.
 
• This type of soil is rich in **potash, phosphoric acid, and lime**, which are beneficial for the cultivation of crops like rice, wheat, sugarcane, and pulses.
 
• Alluvial soils are classified into two types: **Bangar (old alluvium)** and **Khadar (new alluvium)**. Bangar is found on higher plains, while Khadar is deposited along river banks during floods.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Red Clay Soil:**
 
 
• Red soil derives its color from the presence of **iron oxide**.
 
• It is found in southern and eastern India, covering regions of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Odisha, and Andhra Pradesh.
 
• This soil is less fertile due to its low nitrogen, phosphorus, and organic content but can be improved with fertilizers.
 
 
 
• **Black Soil:**
 
 
• Black soil, also called **Regur soil**, is formed from the weathering of volcanic rocks.
 
• It is highly suitable for cultivating **cotton** and is found in states like Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Madhya Pradesh.
 
• It retains moisture well and is rich in **calcium carbonate, magnesium, and potash**.
 
 
 
• **Yellow Clay Soil:**
 
 
• Yellow soil acquires its coloration from **hydrated ferric oxide**.
 
• It is found in dry, semi-arid regions and is less fertile compared to alluvial soil.
 
• The soil is suitable for growing **millets and pulses**.
 
 
 
• **Soil Formation and Deposition:**
 
 
• Soils are formed through the process of **weathering**, which involves breaking down rocks into smaller particles.
 
• River systems like the Indus, Ganges, and Brahmaputra play a crucial role in depositing sediments, shaping the fertile alluvial plains.
 
• Alluvial deposition occurs in **three major regions**: the Indo-Gangetic plains, coastal deltas, and river valleys.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: Lustrous, muddy green patches (patches) in stagnant water bodies are due to the origin of
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Algae**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Algae** are simple, non-flowering aquatic plants that thrive in water bodies, including stagnant ones, and are responsible for green patches seen in such environments.
 
• Algae contain pigments such as **chlorophyll**, which gives them their characteristic green coloration. These pigments allow algae to perform **photosynthesis**.
 
• The growth of algae in stagnant water is often accelerated by the presence of **nutrients** such as phosphates and nitrates from agricultural runoff, sewage, or industrial waste.
 
• These green patches, referred to as **algal blooms**, are common in stagnant water due to the lack of movement, which supports the accumulation of nutrients and sunlight necessary for algal growth.
 
• Excessive algal growth can lead to **eutrophication**, which decreases oxygen levels in the water and adversely affects aquatic life. *Hence, the statement in the question is correct.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of Algae:**
 
 
• Algae can be found in a variety of environments including **freshwater, saltwater, and even on moist soil.**
 
• They range from microscopic forms like **phytoplankton** to larger forms like **seaweeds**.
 
• Common types of algae include **cyanobacteria (blue-green algae), green algae, and diatoms.**
 
• Some algae species are used in industries for **biofuel production, wastewater treatment, and food supplements.**
 
 
 
• **Other Organisms Mentioned in the Options:**
 
 
• **Viruses:** Viruses are infectious agents that require a living host to multiply and are not responsible for green patches in water bodies.
 
• **Parasites:** Parasites live off a host organism and do not contribute to the green coloration observed in stagnant water.
 
• **Fungi:** Fungi are decomposers and usually grow on organic material, not responsible for photosynthesis or green coloration.
 
 
 
• **Eutrophication:**
 
 
• Eutrophication is the process where water bodies become enriched with nutrients, leading to excessive growth of algae.
 
• This phenomenon is common in stagnant water and is often caused by **human activities like agricultural runoff and discharge of untreated sewage.**
 
• Over time, eutrophication can lead to **oxygen depletion**, harming aquatic organisms.
 
 
 
• **Control Measures:**
 
 
• To prevent algal blooms, efforts should be made to reduce nutrient runoff by using **proper wastewater treatment and sustainable farming practices.**
 
• Physical removal of algae and chemical treatments can also be employed, but they should be used cautiously to avoid further environmental impact.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Algal Blooms:**
 
 
• Algal blooms can sometimes produce harmful toxins, leading to phenomena like **red tides** or **blue-green algae blooms**, which are hazardous to humans and marine life.
 
• Monitoring water bodies and reducing nutrient pollution are key to controlling algal blooms.
 
 
</ul
